text: A notebook can tolerate a sloppy except block because you're sitting right there watching it fail. A scheduled script can't — it needs to handle errors deliberately, because nobody's around to notice if it quietly does the wrong thing.

Catch specific exceptions, not a bare except colon. A bare except catches absolutely everything, including a KeyboardInterrupt or a NameError from a typo — things you actually want to see. Catching requests dot exceptions dot Timeout and HTTPError by name means you only handle the failures you anticipated, and anything truly unexpected still surfaces.

Not every failed call should kill the pipeline — a dropped connection or a server hiccup often resolves itself if you just wait and try again. This retries up to max_attempts times, and 2 to the power of attempt gives you exponential backoff: 2 seconds, then 4, then 8, instead of hammering a struggling server at a fixed interval.

Here's the pattern to avoid: catching Exception broadly and quietly falling back to an empty DataFrame. It doesn't crash, but it also silently loads zero rows, and nobody finds out until a report looks wrong days later. The fix is to catch the specific FileNotFoundError, log it as critical, and re-raise — fail fast and loud, exactly when the problem happens.

Wrap a whole pipeline run in try, except, else. On failure, logger dot exception logs the full traceback and then re-raises — and that re-raise matters, because it's what makes the script exit with a non-zero status, which is how cron or Task Scheduler, or a monitoring tool watching for that exit code, actually knows the run failed.

Next up: actually getting this thing to run on its own. You'll schedule the pipeline with cron on Linux and macOS, or Task Scheduler on Windows — and see why things that work fine when you run a script by hand can quietly break once nobody's there to run it.
